ai.definition: Geothermal energy involves harnessing the heat from within the Earth's crust, typically in volcanic or tectonic regions. This method provides a consistent and reliable source of power.
ai.howItWorks: In conventional geothermal systems, wells are drilled to access underground reservoirs of hot water or steam. The heated fluid is brought to the surface where it powers turbines connected to generators, producing electricity. After use, the cooled fluid is reinjected into the ground to maintain the reservoir's pressure and temperature.
ai.problemSolved: Geothermal energy addresses the need for consistent baseload power, which is crucial for maintaining grid stability and reducing reliance on fossil fuels.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves drilling wells, installing heat exchangers, turbines, and generators. This requires specialized equipment and skilled labor.
ai.buildProcess: Construction includes site selection, drilling operations, infrastructure setup (turbines, electrical connections), and system commissioning. The entire build process can take several years from initial planning to operation.
ai.costDrivers: Costs are driven by the depth of drilling required, the complexity of geothermal reservoirs, and the availability of skilled labor and equipment. Exploration risks also contribute significantly to project costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for geothermal energy is positive as it continues to gain recognition for its reliability and environmental benefits. However, significant investment in new projects remains necessary.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally require permits for drilling and operations. Environmental impact assessments are also common due to concerns about induced seismicity and water usage.
ai.risks: Geothermal projects face risks related to exploration uncertainties, high initial costs, potential environmental impacts, and regulatory hurdles. Induced seismic activity is a particular concern in some areas.
ai.profitability: Profitability can vary widely depending on local conditions, energy prices, and government incentives. Projects that receive subsidies or favorable policies tend to be more financially viable.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may see improvements in drilling technologies, enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), and better integration with other renewable sources. Advances could also reduce exploration risks and increase the feasibility of projects in less suitable regions.

subsystems.name: Geothermal reservoir
subsystems.role: a naturally hot, permeable rock formation holding water or steam at depth.

subsystems.name: Wells
subsystems.role: bring hot fluid to the surface and return cooled fluid underground.

subsystems.name: Gathering and separation
subsystems.role: collect fluid from several wells and separate steam from brine.

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: turns steam or hot brine into electricity.

subsystems.name: Cooling and reinjection
subsystems.role: condenses exhaust steam and pumps spent fluid back into the reservoir.

subsystems.name: Grid connection
subsystems.role: delivers electricity to the transmission network.

buildSteps.title: Explore the field
buildSteps.detail: Geological, geochemical and geophysical surveys — including seismic and gravity methods — locate hot permeable rock and estimate the resource.

buildSteps.title: Drill exploration wells
buildSteps.detail: Slim holes, typically 1–2 km deep, confirm temperature and permeability before committing to full-size wells.

buildSteps.title: Drill production and injection wells
buildSteps.detail: Rotary rigs drill 1–3 km deep, often directionally, and line each hole with steel casing cemented in place.

buildSteps.title: Test the wells
buildSteps.detail: Flow tests measure how much fluid each well produces, its temperature, pressure and chemical composition.

buildSteps.title: Build the power plant
buildSteps.detail: Flash-steam or binary-cycle units are erected near the field; binary plants use a secondary working fluid so lower-temperature brine can also be used.

buildSteps.title: Lay pipelines and separators
buildSteps.detail: Insulated pipes connect every wellhead to the plant, with separators removing steam from brine.

buildSteps.title: Commission the plant
buildSteps.detail: The turbine, generator and grid connection are tested and the plant is brought up to full output.

buildSteps.title: Operate and reinject
buildSteps.detail: Spent fluid is pumped back into the reservoir through injection wells to maintain pressure and avoid depleting the field.

pathway.milestone: conventional flash and binary plants in high-temperature volcanic regions such as Iceland, Italy, New Zealand, Kenya and the western United States
pathway.unlocks: firm, low-carbon baseload power that runs day and night.

pathway.milestone: wider use of binary-cycle plants on lower-temperature resources
pathway.unlocks: geothermal power in more regions, including some sedimentary basins.

pathway.milestone: enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) that engineer permeability in hot dry rock
pathway.unlocks: geothermal energy almost anywhere, not just where nature provides a reservoir.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop and superhot-rock systems that drill deeper and hotter
pathway.unlocks: far more power per well and a much larger global resource.
